method: A time charter FFA such as the Capesize 5TC settles on the arithmetic average of the Baltic's daily 5TC assessments in the contract month, in dollars a day; a voyage route FFA such as C3 or C5 on the average of the route's daily assessments, in dollars a tonne (EEX contract specifications, release 047a, July 2026). The 182,000 t ship is hedged in 5TC (182) days, EEX's C5TM; EEX's CPTM settles on the 180,000 t basket, which the guide derives as the 182,000 t basket less USD 3,503 a day (page 77), a fixed difference a CPTM hedge of this ship would carry. Tanker FFAs on ICE settle in dollars a tonne on the average of the month's assessments: the Baltic's for TD3C, TD20, TD22, TD25, TD34, TC2, TC14, TC20 and TC23, Platts' for TC5 and for the 75,000 t Arab Gulf to Japan contract, the TC1 size (ICE Futures Europe rulebook, section TTT), so a TC1 or TC5 cargo priced off the Baltic and hedged on ICE carries the difference between two assessors.

Time charter assessments, and the FFAs that settle on them, are gross daily hire: each 5TC route is assessed at 5 percent total commission (Guide to Market Benchmarks v8.8, pages 77 and 78). A voyage TCE is net of the same commission, so it is grossed up by it before it is set against the 5TC, as the guide does with a voyage's time charter equivalent (section 7.4.3). The basis is that grossed up TCE less the FFA; the freight that earns the FFA is the one whose net TCE equals the FFA less commission; the timing basis is the FFA less the spot 5TC on the fixture date, both gross.

The FFA is the strip over the voyage's days: each day from the fixture date, ballast leg first, is priced at the FFA of its month on the latest curve that could be traded on the fixture date. The hedge is 5TC days equal to the voyage's days, or route FFA tonnes equal to its cargo; the owner keeps 95 percent of what the index pays, so the voyage's days times that share hedge its net earnings exactly.
assumptions: The spot 5TC of 3 July 2026, USD 33,678, is the 180,000 t basis: the BCI of 4,100 and the BDI of 2,717 printed that day fit a 182,000 t basket of 37,181 (that figure plus the guide's 3,503, page 77), and not 33,678 itself, which would give a BCI of 3,713. The study prices the 182,000 t ship and sets it against 37,181.
